title: Aged about 12, Mary Anning helped find a giant sea reptile in the cliffs of Lyme Regis

cover.alt: Mary Anning, in a bonnet and plaid shawl with a hammer, stands below grey cliffs beside a fossil skull in the rock; her small black-and-white dog sits nearby.

body: **Mary Anning** (1799–1847) hunted fossils in the crumbling cliffs at Lyme Regis to keep her poor family. With her brother Joseph she found the first largely complete ichthyosaur to be described by scientists, and in 1823 the first nearly complete plesiosaur, a beast so strange that the great anatomist Georges Cuvier at first suspected a fake. The Geological Society admitted no women until 1919 and she often went without credit for her finds, but in 2010 the Royal Society named her among the ten British women who most influenced science.

slides.alt: Below towering grey layered cliffs, a boy in a cap points up at a long-snouted fossil skull with a huge eye socket set in the rock. A girl in a bonnet with a basket looks on.
slides.caption: Lyme Regis, autumn 1811. Mary Anning's brother Joseph finds a skull about 4 feet long in the cliffs. Mary is 12. Scientists say: crocodile.

slides.alt: On the beach a long skeleton lies exposed on a slab: a long snout, a spine, ribs and paddles. A workman with a pick helps; Mary points at it.
slides.caption: About a year later Mary, now around 13, digs out the rest: a skeleton about 5 metres long. It is not a crocodile.

bubbles.text: With paddles? Funny sort of crocodile.
bubbles.speaker: Mary Anning

slides.alt: Outside a small cottage, Mary stands behind a table of fossils: coiled ammonites, belemnites and bones. A lady in a bonnet points at one; her husband in a top hat waits.
slides.caption: Fossils pay the rent. The Annings sell “curiosities” to visitors from a table by their home, and the big skeleton fetches £23.

bubbles.text: Snakestones, ma'am. Every home should have one.
bubbles.speaker: Mary Anning

slides.alt: On a slab on the shore lies a skeleton with a tiny head on an immensely long neck, a barrel body and four paddles. Mary, now a woman, stands over it with her dog.
slides.caption: 10 December 1823: Mary, 24, finds a stranger beast still: a tiny head on an immensely long neck. It is a plesiosaur.

bubbles.text: Well. Nobody is going to believe this.
bubbles.speaker: Mary Anning

slides.alt: In a study with shelves of skulls, the grey-haired anatomist Georges Cuvier studies a drawing of the long-necked skeleton.
slides.caption: In Paris, Georges Cuvier, the greatest anatomist of the day, sees a drawing. He has a theory: a fake, made from two animals.

bubbles.text: Such a neck? Clearly two animals stuck together.
bubbles.speaker: Georges Cuvier

slides.alt: In a dark panelled room, gentlemen in black coats gather round the plesiosaur fossil on a board, one pointing at it.
slides.caption: Letters and drawings from British geologists convince Cuvier it is real. The gentlemen discuss it at length. The finder is not invited.

bubbles.text: A splendid specimen. Who found it?
bubbles.speaker: A geologist

slides.alt: Rocks and dust crash down the cliff in a landslide. Mary runs clear, looking back and shouting.
slides.caption: October 1833: a landslide comes down. Mary escapes, but her dog Tray is killed “in a moment before my eyes”, she writes.

slides.alt: Mary, older, stands on the beach at sunset with her hammer and basket below the cliffs.
slides.caption: In 1844 she tells a visiting German doctor about her fame. She dies three years later, aged 47. The Geological Society admits women in 1919.

bubbles.text: I am well known throughout the whole of Europe.
bubbles.speaker: Mary Anning

slides.question: Why did Georges Cuvier at first doubt Anning's plesiosaur?
slides.explanation: A tiny head on such a long neck was unlike any animal he knew, so he suspected it was two skeletons put together. Letters and drawings convinced him.

source.label: Natural History Museum: Mary Anning, the unsung hero
